rationale: A wins because it gives the founder three genuinely different reporting routes: regulatory access, profitability/expansion tension, and US market transfer. Its strongest line, "Monzo returns to the US — this time renting a banking license instead of chasing one," is a real beat story with a real missing proof item. B is useful, but it splits the profit story into two near-neighbors and leans on an imported thesis: "The widely-held belief this cuts against: challenger banks burn cash, struggle to make money at scale, and have repeatedly failed to crack the US." That may be true, but it was not in the facts, and a pitch built on unsourced category wisdom is where founders go to die in inboxes.
gaps_in_A: "Monzo posted its first annual profit — then spent it on a second shot at America" overstates causality. The facts support sequence, not that profit funded the US move.
"renting a banking license" is sharp, but a little loose. Through a partner bank is the fact; renting a license is the copywriter putting on sunglasses indoors.
Angle two needs the actual profit figure. A names that gap, but without it the business-model angle is still more promising than pitchable.
gaps_in_B: "The widely-held belief this cuts against: challenger banks burn cash, struggle to make money at scale, and have repeatedly failed to crack the US" imports a category premise not supplied in the update.
"what the partner-bank model gives up (economics, control, branding)" is plausible, but not grounded in the facts. It should be framed strictly as questions, not asserted tradeoffs.

Angles two and three both orbit the same profit/CAC gap. "A UK challenger bank turned its first annual profit" and "Monzo's first profitable year, by the numbers" are not different enough to both earn space.

"run `newsjack-detector` first to confirm there's no fresher challenger-bank news" is process clutter. The immediate next step is sourcing the missing profit figure, partner bank, and US rollout numbers.
